To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the SLIP model is a valid abstraction of running with a segmented leg, (ii) the operational space controller allows for a direct application of the SLIP control to a real leg, (iii) a compensation method allows for a direct use of existing dead-beats, (iv) the compensation method reduces the minimal running speed and increases the stable running region.
the SLIP running model can be used as a reference model for running robots, and that a dead-beat control strategy is sufficient to generate running behavior in a real robot.
the SLIP model can be directly projected to the dynamics of an articulated leg and that this projection leads to a significant increase in the region of stable running.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of how to transfer knowledge from the simple SLIP model to a real robot.
the question of how a robot can run like an animal and how the resulting behavior can be exploited for efficient, energy-saving locomotion.
the question: How can we transfer the findings from SLIP running models to real robots, and how can we use this knowledge to improve the performance of real robots?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our approach allows the direct application to arbitrary robotic leg designs, while the SLIP model provides a powerful tool for the analysis and design of such controllers.
SLIP is a very good model to describe the behavior of the leg during running.
the SLIP model is not only a good abstraction of legged locomotion, but also provides a solid basis to control real robotic legs.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we show how the SLIP model can be used to design a simple controller to stabilize running in real robots, even if the leg has no passive compliance.
the proposed method enables us to directly apply existing SLIP control strategies to arbitrary legged robots.
we show how to exploit the insights gained by the simple SLIP model in a real robot with a segmented leg, and how to extend the model to account for the energetic losses due to the impact collisions.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the SLIP model can be used to generate running motions on real robots without any need for a detailed model of the actual robot, and without requiring any adaptation of the SLIP controller.
the SLIP model is an effective tool to understand and control the dynamics of a wide variety of legged systems.
the SLIP running model can be directly applied to robotic legs with a minimum of additional effort.
